t: the people were accustomed, etc.. See Hilchot Tefillah 7:11.
the portion Tzav. The portion of the command about the Tamid offering (Numbers 28:1-9).
and the priestly blessing. The verses of the blessing "May the Lord bless you and keep you," etc. (Numbers 6:24-26).
this mishnah. Tractate Peah 1:1.
that have no measure. For which no specific amount was given for fulfilling the commandment.
peah. Leaving the edge of the field uncut and leaving it for the poor (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim chapters 1-3).
and first fruits. Separating the first of the fruits and giving them to the priests in the Temple (Hilchot Bikkurim chapters 2-4).
and appearance. The commandment to come to the Temple on the three pilgrimage festivals and bring a burnt offering (Hilchot Chagigah chapters 1-2).
and acts of kindness. Helping others.
whose fruits one eats. He profits from them.
and the principal remains for him in the World to Come. The substance of the mitzvah remains intact for the World to Come, even though he already enjoys its profits in this world.
honoring father and mother, etc.. All are commandments between a person and his fellow, and their fulfillment benefits a person's life in this world.
and Torah study is equal to them all. It is equivalent to all of them.
Rabbi Zeira said, etc.. A statement from the Talmud (Berakhot 31a and elsewhere), which appears there as an example of a ruling from within which one should pray (see Hilchot Tefillah 4:18).

that even if they see a drop of blood like a mustard seed, etc.. Although sometimes by strict law seven clean days are not required, they adopted the stringency of acting as the law of a zavah, so as not to come to stumble (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 11:4).
the school of Elijah taught, etc.. This is the last baraita in the Babylonian Talmud (Niddah 73a), and speaks in praise of engaging in halakhot.
he has the world to come. And it is expounded that one who learns halakhot ("halikhot") merits the World to Come ("olam lo").
Rabbi Elazar said, etc.. This statement appears at the conclusion of several tractates of the Babylonian Talmud and speaks in praise of Torah scholars.
a person should always, etc.. From Midrash Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah chapter 21.
fear Heaven in secret. Even when no one sees him.
and acknowledge the truth. Agree with the truth, and retract if he erred.
and speak truth in his heart. That his speech is not merely lip service but that he believes it in his heart.
what are we, etc.. Surely we and our deeds have no value before the Creator.
and men of renown. The famous people.
as if without knowledge. As if they do not know.
but we, etc.. Despite what was said above about the lowliness of man and his deeds, there is a special bond between God and Israel, which gives meaning to their existence.
You are He before the world was created, etc.. This is a continuation of the words in Tanna Devei Eliyahu, which expands on the declaration of God's unity mentioned in the first verse of the Shema.
sanctify Your great and holy name in Your world, and by Your salvation exalt and raise our horn. That Your kingship be revealed by raising the horn of Israel and saving us.

the first blessing, etc.. An introductory blessing to the recitation of praise, in which it says that they will praise God through the psalms written by King David, and to which are added many blessings on the Creator's ways of conduct and deeds; see Hilchot Tefillah 7:12.
darkness. Darkness.
and he reads these verses, etc.. Verses mostly from the book of Psalms, about praises of God for His greatness and for His choosing the people of Israel.
"A psalm of praise by David," etc.. A psalm of praise to God for His greatness and kindnesses, whose verses are arranged in alphabetical order.
until the end of the book of Psalms. Which are five more chapters of praise, beginning and ending with the word "Halleluyah."
the last blessing, etc.. It is the concluding blessing for the chapters of praise, which says that it is fitting to use every language of praise to glorify the Creator.
for to You it is fitting. So it is proper that it be done in Your honor.
and he reads the Song... according to the custom of the place. In some places they were accustomed to read the Song of the Sea or the Song of Ha'azinu (see Hilchot Tefillah 7:13).
Nishmat Kol Chai, etc.. A special, detailed prayer of praise, which describes the greatness of God, the human inability to praise Him properly, and the obligation to do so nonetheless.
in earlier times. In the past.
You have drawn us up. You raised us up to redemption.
that You have divided. You divided the limbs, each with its own function.
"A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day," the whole psalm. Which deals with the future Sabbath, the time when the justice in God's acts will be revealed.
and on Yom Kippur. Which is also called "a Sabbath of complete rest" (Leviticus 16:31, 23:32).
the Great Hallel. A song of praise to God's greatness and kindnesses to Israel, and each of the praises mentioned in it ends with the refrain "for His kindness endures forever" (Psalms chapter 136).
the Songs of Ascents. Psalms beginning "A Song of Ascents" (chapters 120-134).

the first blessing before the morning Shema. A blessing of praise for the creation of the luminaries, mentioning the praise that the angels on high offer for the renewal of creation (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 1:6-7).
and to those who dwell. And to those who live on it.
Your possessions. Things You created that belong to You.
the leaders of the hosts of the holy ones, who exalt the Almighty. The heads of the camps of holy angels who exalt God.
to the blessed God they offer sweet melodies. To the blessed God they will sing sweetly.
Ahavat Olam. A blessing of thanks for God's love for us, and requests flowing from it regarding Torah study, God's kingship over Israel, and the ingathering of the exiles.
Emet VeYatziv, etc.. A blessing of declaration of God's unity, and thanks that God redeems us in every generation and especially for the redemption from Egypt.
besides You. Other than You.
the ends of the earth. The extremities of the earth.
who brings on evenings. A blessing of praise for God's control over the changes of the times of day.
who opens gates. The gates of the heavens.
the Lord of hosts is His name. For He is king over the host of heaven.
Ahavat Olam. A blessing of thanks for God's love for us, and for our connection with Him through Torah study.
crown. Crown.
Emet Emunah, etc.. A blessing of declaration of faith in God, and thanks that God redeems us in every generation and especially for the redemption from Egypt.
in His wrath. In His anger.
Hashkivenu, etc.. A blessing for protection at night, with the addition of verses of blessing, thanksgiving and enthroning.
1) and who possesses all. That everything belongs to Him.
shield of Abraham. Protects Abraham and his descendants.
2) mighty forever. Possessing infinite power.
sustains. Provides livelihood and food.
and keeps His faith to those who sleep in the dust. Fulfills His promise to revive the dead.
3) and holy ones. The angels, who are called holy, and Israel too are called so.
9) our year. This year and its produce.
and satisfy. Grant satiety.
and water the face of the world. Irrigate the earth of the world.
a future and a hope. A good end and the fulfillment of expectations.
10) and raise a banner. Lift a flag.
15) the shoot of David. A name for the Messiah, who is from the descendants of King David.
17) and turn to their prayer. Accept their prayer.
and restore the service. The Temple service.
and the fire-offerings of Israel. The offerings of Israel, burned in the fire of the altar.
Your dwelling. Your house.
as of old. As in the past.
18) all the living. All creatures.
19) from the light of Your countenance. The revelation of kindness and favor from on high.
in the days of the sun, etc.. See Hilchot Tefillah 2:15-16.
on Saturday night, etc.. See Hilchot Tefillah 2:12.
Ya'aleh VeYavo. A prayer for festivals, which is a request to be remembered before God on these days. See Hilchot Tefillah 2:10-11.
on this day of holy convocation. For the festivals are called "holy convocations."
Aneinu, etc.. A request that God answer us on the fast day; see Hilchot Tefillah 2:14.
Rachem, etc.. An addition that mentions mourning for Jerusalem and a request for mercy on it; see Hilchot Tefillah 2:14.
and the legions swallowed it up. Armies of enemies conquered it.

for You, Lord, founded it with fire. You built Jerusalem with fire, with the revelation of fire at the dedication of the Temple (see II Chronicles 5:13-14). In other versions: "for You, Lord, kindled it with fire," based on the verse "The Lord has spent His wrath, He poured out His fierce anger, and kindled a fire in Zion that consumed its foundations" (Lamentations 4:11), and corresponding to this He will in the future rebuild it with fire, protect it as a wall of fire, and dwell in it.
Al HaNissim. An addition that thanks for the miracle that happened at that time; see Hilchot Tefillah 2:13.
we will sanctify You and revere You. A call to sanctify God's name in the world as the angels do (see Hilchot Tefillah 9:4).
he reads with them. The prayer leader says them together with the congregation.
the holy King. See Hilchot Tefillah 2:18.
Kaddish. A prayer of praise that God's name be magnified and blessed in the world.
forever. Always.
Seder HaYom. Verses of sanctification with their translation that are said after the supplications of Nefilat Apayim (see Hilchot Tefillah 9:5-6).
and when he finishes reading the Torah. See ibid. 12:20-22.

"Yitgadal veyitkadash... le'alma ule'almei almaya". May His great name be magnified and sanctified, in the world He created by His will, and may He establish His kingdom, bring forth His salvation, bring near His messiah and redeem His people. In your lifetime and in your days and in the lifetime of the entire House of Israel, speedily and soon, and say Amen! May His great name be blessed forever and for all eternity.

"Shmei dekudsha berikh hu... da'amiran be'alma ve'imru amen". The name of the Holy One, blessed be He, is far above all the blessings, songs, praises and consolations uttered in the world, and say Amen!
with all of a person's strength. See Hilchot Tefillah 9:1.
last. Final.
and they depart. They go on their way.

"Titkabal tzelotkhon... ve'al kol kehalhon deYisrael ve'imru amen". May your prayer be accepted and your request granted, and the prayer and request of the entire House of Israel before their Father in heaven. May there be great peace from heaven, and help and salvation upon you and upon us and upon the entire congregation of Israel, and say Amen!
Kaddish DeRabbanan. Kaddish with a blessing for the Sages.

"Yitgadal veyitkadash... veyifrok amei". May His great name be magnified and sanctified, He who will in the future renew the world and revive the dead and save the living, and rebuild the city of Jerusalem, and establish the holy Temple, and uproot idolatry from the earth, and restore the service of Heaven (some read: "Shemeih" - His name) to its place in its light and glory, and may He establish His kingdom, bring forth His salvation, hasten His messiah and redeem His people.

"Al rabbanan ve'al talmideihon... di vishmaya ve'imru amen". For the Sages and for their disciples and for the disciples of their disciples who engage in Torah, in this place and in every place, may they and you have grace, kindness, mercy, help and relief from before their Father in heaven, and say Amen!
in Nefilat Apayim. See Hilchot Tefillah 5:14, 7:17-18, 9:5.
and for My praise I will restrain My anger for you, that I not cut you off. For the sake of My praise I will be patient and not destroy you.
keep this forever, etc.. Remember forever the good will of Your people, and direct their hearts to You.
"Blessed be the Lord who daily bears our burden, the God of our salvation, Selah". Every day God constantly bestows His goodness upon us.
those who go astray. Those who have lost their way.
that we not toil in vain nor bear children for terror. That our effort and labor not be in vain and for ruin.
the song, a psalm that the Levites would say in the Temple on that day. For on each day of the week they said a different psalm from Psalms (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 6:9).
"Of David, to You, Lord, I lift up my soul". Which is a psalm of repentance and request for help.
Rabbi Elazar said, etc.. As above in the opening of the prayer for each day, 1.

"There is none like our God, none like our Lord, etc.". In some manuscripts the continuation appears: There is none like our King, none like our Savior. Who is like our God, who is like our Lord, who is like our King, who is like our Savior. We will thank our God, we will thank our Lord, we will thank our King, we will thank our Savior. Blessed is our God, blessed is our Lord, blessed is our King, blessed is our Savior. You are our God, You are our Lord, You are our King, You are our Savior. You will arise and have mercy on Zion, for it is time to be gracious to her, for the appointed time has come.
crown. Crown.

You commanded Moses on Mount Sinai the commandment of the Sabbath, remember and keep. "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy" (Exodus 20:8) and "Keep the Sabbath day to sanctify it" (Deuteronomy 5:12), which were said at the Sinai revelation.
the day of rest. The Sabbath day.
You did not give it, our King, to the nations of the lands. The rest of the Sabbath day.
a crown of praise and a splendor of salvation. Terms of praise for the Sabbath.
grant us, our Father, etc.. Help us that our rest be complete, without troubles.
and bestow on us, Lord our God, the blessing of Your festivals. Bless us with the special blessing of the festival.
that You return and have mercy on it. On the Temple.
priests to their service. The Temple service.
and Levites to their platform. On which they sang in the Temple (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:6).
and Israel to their station. Representatives of Israel present in the Temple at the time of offering the sacrifices (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 6:1).
most of the people were accustomed, etc.. See Hilchot Tefillah 2:19.
a widespread custom, etc.. See Hilchot Tefillah 2:19.
and the preparing of a lamp for the son of Jesse, Your anointed. Giving honor to the Davidic kingship.
and its iniquity will shut its mouth. Wickedness will close its mouth and will have no influence.
and the arrogant kingdom. The joyful one, confident in its strength.
and was ashamed. Was put to shame.
and before His elders glory. When the Lord reigns in Jerusalem, honor will be given to the elders of Israel who cling to God.

the first blessing, etc.. In the Musaf of Rosh Hashanah special blessings are prayed, and after each blessing the shofar is blown (see Hilchot Tefillah 2:6, Hilchot Shofar 3:6-8). The first blessing is "Malkhuyot," and its subject is acknowledging God's kingship in the world. In this blessing the sanctity of the day is also mentioned.
I will wait for God. I will hope for the Lord.
I will entreat His face. I will appease Him.
to establish the world under the kingship of the Almighty. To establish a world that acknowledges God's kingship.
today is the birth of the world. Today the world's gestation was completed; today it was created.
the second blessing. It is "Zikhronot," and its subject is that God remembers all the deeds of the world, and the binding of Isaac and His covenant with the patriarchs.
many deeds. In all the actions that were done.
without end. Without limit.
from the beginning You made this known, etc.. The matter has been known from ancient times.
the third blessing. It is "Shofarot," and its subject is enthroning God with the shofar, and His revelation in this sound.
in the mists of purity. At the giving of the Torah the Divine Presence was revealed in a cloud.
of the day of the fast of Yom Kippur. See Hilchot Tefillah 2:7.
as they are written in the Torah. In the portion of Pinchas in the book of Numbers (chapters 28-29; see Hilchot Tefillah 13:14).
the text of the confession. The Yom Kippur confession, said on the eve of Yom Kippur and after each of the five prayers of the day (see Hilchot Teshuvah 2:7-8, and see also Hilchot Tefillah 6:2).

HaRachaman, etc.. In all Jewish communities it was customary to add further requests beginning with "HaRachaman." Some add a blessing that the guest gives the host (see Maimonides, Hilchot Berakhot 7:2).
who feeds the world. The blessing "HaZan," the first blessing of Birkat HaMazon. A blessing of thanks for the goodness of God who sustains the world.

we thank You. The blessing "HaAretz," the second blessing of Birkat HaMazon (for details of its text see Hilchot Berakhot 2:3). Thanks for the bestowal of the Land of Israel, and for the food that comes from it.

have mercy. The blessing "Boneh Yerushalayim," the third blessing of Birkat HaMazon (for details of its text see ibid. 2:4). A request for mercy for the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Davidic kingship.
the God, our Father, our King... the Good and Doer of good. The fourth blessing, instituted by the Sages of the Mishnah (Hilchot Berakhot 2:1). Thanks for all the good that God bestows on us.
who chose good prophets. A blessing of praise for God's choosing of the Torah, Israel and the prophets (see Hilchot Tefillah 12:15).
the God who is faithful in all His words. That all the words of prophecy are true and are fulfilled.
who builds Jerusalem. A plea for mercy on Israel and on Jerusalem.
Shield of David. A request for the restoration of David's kingship to its former strength.

according to the text with which he concludes the middle blessing of the prayer on that day. By mentioning the sanctity of Israel and the sanctity of the occasion (see above, the middle blessings on Shabbatot and festivals). For example, on a Shabbat that is Rosh Chodesh one blesses 'Who sanctifies the Shabbat, Israel and the new moons' (see Hilchot Tefillah 12:15).
the topics that most of the people are accustomed to read from the Prophets each Shabbat. For the haftarot of the festivals and special days, see Hilchot Tefillah 13:4-20.

Jethro heard; In the year that King Uzziah died, etc. until the one who increases the government, etc.. Today the custom is not to read all these verses, but to read a passage beginning where the Rambam indicates (until 6:13 or 7:6, according to the different customs), and then to skip and read a passage from the end (9:5-6; according to the Sephardic custom this passage is not read). Perhaps this is also the Rambam's intent.
And these are the ordinances; The word that came to Jeremiah. Instead of 34:8 one may cite 35:1.

Command Aaron; Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, etc. until for in these I delight, says the Lord. Today the custom is not to read all these verses, but to read a passage beginning where the Rambam indicates (until 7:28 or 8:3, according to the different customs), and then to skip and read a passage from the end (9:22-23). Perhaps this is also the Rambam's intent.
in which two portions are read. On a Shabbat on which two weekly portions are read together, in order to complete the cycle of portions each year (Hilchot Tefillah 13:2).
they conclude with the consolations. See Hilchot Tefillah 13:19. Likewise, on the three Shabbatot before the Ninth of Av they were accustomed to read words of rebuke (ibid.).

the topics that most of the people are accustomed to read, etc.. There are different customs among the communities and congregations regarding the verses of the haftarah read each Shabbat, as they appear in the printed Chumashim.

Note:. In the Rambam's order of prayers there are many differences from the text of prayer accepted in most communities (except for the Yemenites, whose text is similar to the Rambam's). In general, the text of the prayer divides into the Ashkenazic custom and the Sephardic custom, and the Ashkenazim are themselves divided into two main versions called 'Nusach Ashkenaz' and 'Nusach Sefarad' (for the whole subject see the Appendix: 'The Different Versions of the Prayer', p. 766). Below we will not note every difference between the versions, only the main differences between them.

Blessed is He who sanctifies His name among the multitudes. The custom of most communities is to conclude without mentioning the Name. In some Ashkenazic communities they were accustomed to conclude with mentioning the Name (see Taz, Orach Chayim 46:9, and Aruch HaShulchan 46:16).

the first blessing that is said before the verses of praise. According to the Ashkenazic and Sephardic custom, before 'Baruch She'amar' they say the verses about the offerings, the chapter 'Eizehu Mekoman', and the baraita of 'Rabbi Yishmael says' (see Hilchot Tefillah 7:12, Rulings and Views), and after them they say the 'Kaddish d'Rabbanan' (see below, Kaddish and the Conclusion of the Prayer, 4). Afterwards they add the 'Hodu' verses (I Chronicles 16:8-36 and additional verses) and 'A Psalm, a Song for the Dedication of the House' (Psalm 30). According to Nusach Ashkenaz they say the 'Hodu' verses after 'Baruch She'amar', and they also say Kaddish after 'A Psalm, a Song for the Dedication of the House'.

Blessed is He who removes darkness and brings light, etc.. According to the Sephardic and Ashkenazic custom, these words of praise are not said: 'Blessed is He who removes darkness...' and 'Blessed is He before whom there is no forgetting or ...'.

May the glory of the Lord endure forever; May the Lord rejoice in His works. According to the Sephardic and Ashkenazic custom, they say 'A Psalm of Thanksgiving' (Psalm 100) before the verses of 'Yehi Kevod'. The Rema (Orach Chayim 51:9) wrote that it is not to be said on Shabbatot and festivals, nor on the eve of Pesach, on Chol HaMoed Pesach, or on the eve of Yom Kippur, because the thanksgiving offering is not brought at these times. Some refrain from saying it only on Shabbatot and festivals (Kaf HaChayim).

and exalted above all blessing and praise. According to the Sephardic and Ashkenazic version, they say the rest of the chapter in Nehemiah up to 'and You cast their pursuers into the depths like a stone into mighty waters', and afterwards they say the verses of 'Vayosha Hashem' (Exodus 14:30-31) and the Song of the Sea that follows them (see next, and see Hilchot Tefillah 7:13).

and they were also accustomed to read 'A Psalm, a Song', etc.. According to the Sephardic custom and Nusach Sefarad, they say these additions before the blessing 'Baruch She'amar', and according to Nusach Ashkenaz they are said after this blessing. In all the versions they say further psalms beyond these additions.
